intake-408.title: Episodic Memories Generation and Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
key_claims: Measures how effectively LLMs encode, store, and retrieve episodic events within extended narratives (10K-1M tokens)
Even SOTA models (GPT-5 0.942, Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.968) show significant gaps in chronological awareness (0.80 best) versus near-perfect recall
Dual-metric evaluation: Simple Recall Score (F1 by matching event count groups) and Chronological Awareness Score (latest-state + Kendall tau ordering)
Synthetic narratives with controlled ground truth avoid data contamination — 11 datasets across 4 styles, 3 lengths
Fine-tuning fails to embed episodic knowledge — merely overfits to single learned facts without temporal/relational understanding

claim_corrections.note: The 10K-1M range is real and the 1M QA parquet is on our disk, but the paper reports NO 1M results — the very-long book is footnote 3 plus an additional_million.ipynb, and the README's own table marks its "used in" column "/". Cite the range as "datasets span 10K-1M; published results cover 10K and 100K".

THREE corrections. (a) Best chronological is 0.817 (gemini-2.5-flash), not 0.80 — the entry took the value from the models it happened to name. (b) These figures are README leaderboard values from Sept 2025, NOT ICLR 2025 paper results; the paper evaluates GPT-4/Claude/Llama-3.1/o1-mini. Never attribute gpt-5 or claude-sonnet-4 numbers to the paper. (c) "near-perfect recall" applies to the top three only; the leaderboard spans 0.300-0.968.

The dual-metric description is accurate and is what our adapter implements — but "Simple Recall Score" and "Chronological Awareness Score" appear ZERO times in arXiv v1. They are README/leaderboard names for a post-paper aggregation of the paper's per-group lenient F1 (Table 3) and Kendall tau (Table 4). Cite the README for the composite scores and the paper for the underlying F1/tau. CRUCIAL RIDER: the paper's F1 uses an LLM SEMANTIC MATCHER (Appendix B.3.1/B.4); our f1_list replaces it with token-F1. Our scores are on OUR scale, never on the leaderboard's.

11 datasets and 3 lengths CONFIRMED. "4 styles" is wrong — there are 3 book styles (default, world news, sci-fi) plus ordered and gpt-4o-generated VARIATIONS. The 4 is the number of Figshare data directories, which is also exactly the four variant dirs on our disk. Say "11 datasets across 4 released variant directories, 3 book styles, 3 lengths".

Confirmed verbatim in the conclusion and quantified in Section 5.2 and Table 3 (fine-tuned gpt-4o-mini: 0.00 on the hallucination bin, 0.83 on single-event, decaying to 0.19 at 6+ events). This is the entry's strongest and most transferable claim, and intake-814 already leans on it — keep it exactly as written.

intake-1333.title: The Harness Effect: How Orchestration Design Sets the Token Economics of Enterprise Agentic AI
intake-1333.claim_01: EFFICIENCY IS MODEL-INVARIANT, QUALITY IS NOT. Every one of six models gets cheaper, -33% (Gemini 3.1) to -61% (Flash 3.5), no exception (Table 4); mean quality gain per model correlates with baseline strength at r=0.99, n=6 ("harness leverage", Section 6.4: Palmyra +0.079, Sonnet +0.073, Qwen -0.031). Of 48 capability x model cells, 30 improve, 11 flat, 7 regress, and all 7 regressions are on the three smaller models concentrated in orchestration-heavy capabilities (Section 6.3). The one net-new capability, sub-agent delegation, has a CAPABILITY FLOOR: 0.86/0.85 on the two strongest models but 0.42-0.45 on the fast tier (Table 5).

claim_correction_01.note: Table 4, Section 6.4 and Table 5 verified cell by cell. Narrowing to remember when citing: r=0.99 is over six points and the authors call it suggestive; the sub-agent floor row has no baseline arm at all.

intake-1333.reported_results_item_06: Appendix A Table 6, 48 cells; worst regressions MCP tool use Qwen 3.6 .65->.50 (-0.15) and GLM 5.1 .72->.66; largest gains GDR Palmyra .79->.91 and Sonnet .80->.90, MCP Sonnet .78->.88 and Palmyra .78->.88.
